Measured relations and operator algebras

Borel carriers and uniform wandering neighborhoods

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Author self-check in progress; not independently reviewed. New original text is public domain (CC0).

Introduction

A continuous free action separates a point from all its translates by a compact family avoiding the identity. To obtain a positive measurable wandering set, one needs a point where the original positive set has positive measure in every neighborhood. That point can be found without assuming that the measure is Radon.

This distinction sharpens Takesaki III, XIII.1, Exercise 5. Part (a) asks for a positive compact subset of a given Borel set. Part (b) separates a support point from a compact family of translates. Part (c) asks for measurable compact wandering freeness. We prove part (c) at the printed finite, quasi-invariant, ergodic, full-support topological scope, retaining the chapter's separable locally compact group convention. We do not assume a countable base for the space or Radon regularity in that proof.

For part (a), we give the complete regularity theorem and application when every open set is sigma-compact, including the second countable locally compact case. The exercise block states a general countability convention, “such as separability,” without explicitly choosing a countable base for its topological space. A countable dense set alone is not substituted for that stronger topological hypothesis. We give a complete disposition of the distinct scopes: positive compact extraction holds under the stronger regularity hypothesis and in the atomic standard branch, while Theorem 3.29 gives an atomless counterexample under CH for ordinary separability and an actual conull standard Borel measure. The printed convention does not specify a unique intended topology. The complete part (c) proof holds throughout.

Compact fixed sets and free Polish models, Lemmas 2.1–2.2, proves all three intended assertions for finite Radon measures on arbitrary locally compact Hausdorff spaces. We preserve that proof and now prove the regularity input explicitly, then supply a second argument which bypasses compact extraction for the measurable conclusion. Free actions and the crossed-product diagonal, Definition in Section 4, fixes the compact projection condition. The underlying group action here is an actual jointly continuous point action; every nonidentity element fixes no point.

We use Hausdorff topology, compactness, countable additivity, continuity of measure along monotone sequences, and basic countable ordinal arithmetic. General standard-form, modular and weight theory is not used. Measured covariant-system interpretations retain the chapter's standard sigma-finite background. The atomic branch below uses only countable point separation on a conull standard Borel subspace and proves all three source clauses in that branch. The atomless standard-measure case is treated by the full CH construction below. CH is explicit; existence of such a counterexample without CH is not claimed.

Theorem 3.5 (the full atomic branch of source Exercise 5). Retain the finite quasi-invariant ergodic measure and pointwise free action of Section 3, and suppose the measure is standard in the preceding sense. Compact inner regularity is not an additional premise.

Proof. Lemma 3.4 supplies one point of positive mass. Quasi-invariance gives μ({gx})>0\mu(\{gx\})>0μ({gx})>0 if and only if μ({x})>0\mu(\{x\})>0μ({x})>0. Consequently DDD is exactly invariant. It is nonnull, so ergodicity makes it conull.

The orbit OOO is then a countable Borel set, exactly invariant and nonnull, so ergodicity makes it conull. A positive EEE has E∩O≠∅E\cap O\ne\varnothingE∩O=∅. Choose xxx there. It has positive mass; its singleton is compact in the original topology, and freeness gives gx≠xgx\ne xgx=x for every g≠eg\ne eg=e. This proves (3.7).

Every neighborhood of xxx has positive intersection with L={x}L=\{x\}L={x}, so xxx is the density point for part (b). Lemma 3.1 separates it uniformly from any prescribed compact K⊂G∖{e}K\subset G\setminus\{e\}K⊂G∖{e}. For part (c), q=1{x}q=\mathbf1_{\{x\}}q=1{x}​ is a nonzero projection below 1E\mathbf1_E1E​, with qαg(q)=0q\alpha_g(q)=0qαg​(q)=0 for every nonidentity ggg, hence for every such compact family. □\square□

Corollary 3.6 (the unresolved branch is atomless). At the full standard-measure source scope, either the measure is atomless or Theorem 3.5 proves all three clauses. In particular an uncountable GGG forces the measure to be atomless.

Proof. A finite measure that is not atomless has a positive measure atom by definition. Lemma 3.4 and Theorem 3.5 apply, and their countability conclusion excludes this alternative when GGG is uncountable. The atomless alternative is retained even for countable groups; its compact-extraction step is not proved by this dichotomy. □\square□

Lemma 3.7 (a maximal compact remainder). Let μ\muμ be a finite Borel measure on a Hausdorff space and let EEE be Borel. Put r(E)=sup⁡{μ(C):C⊂E, C compact}.(3.9) r(E)=\sup\{\mu(C):C\subset E,\ C\text{ compact}\}. \tag{3.9} r(E)=sup{μ(C):C⊂E, C compact}.(3.9) There is a Borel F⊂EF\subset EF⊂E such that μ(F)=μ(E)−r(E),μ(C)=0for every compact C⊂F.(3.10) \mu(F)=\mu(E)-r(E),\qquad \mu(C)=0\quad\text{for every compact }C\subset F. \tag{3.10} μ(F)=μ(E)−r(E),μ(C)=0for every compact C⊂F.(3.10) Consequently, the assertion that every positive Borel subset of EEE contains a positive compact subset is equivalent to compact inner regularity on every Borel subset of EEE.

Proof. Choose compact Cn⊂EC_n\subset ECn​⊂E with μ(Cn)→r(E)\mu(C_n)\to r(E)μ(Cn​)→r(E); if r(E)=0r(E)=0r(E)=0, take Cn=∅C_n=\varnothingCn​=∅. The finite unions Dn=⋃j≤nCjD_n=\bigcup_{j\le n}C_jDn​=⋃j≤n​Cj​ are compact and contained in EEE. Their masses are at most r(E)r(E)r(E) and at least μ(Cn)\mu(C_n)μ(Cn​), so μ(Dn)→r(E)\mu(D_n)\to r(E)μ(Dn​)→r(E). Thus D=⋃nDnD=\bigcup_nD_nD=⋃n​Dn​ is Borel with μ(D)=r(E)\mu(D)=r(E)μ(D)=r(E). Set F=E∖DF=E\setminus DF=E∖D. If C⊂FC\subset FC⊂F is compact, then C∩Dn=∅C\cap D_n=\varnothingC∩Dn​=∅ and C∪DnC\cup D_nC∪Dn​ is a compact subset of EEE. Hence μ(C)+μ(Dn)≤r(E).(3.11) \mu(C)+\mu(D_n)\le r(E). \tag{3.11} μ(C)+μ(Dn​)≤r(E).(3.11) Letting n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞ gives μ(C)=0\mu(C)=0μ(C)=0 and proves (3.10).

For the consequence, apply this construction to any Borel H⊂EH\subset EH⊂E. If r(H)<μ(H)r(H)<\mu(H)r(H)<μ(H), its positive remainder contradicts the asserted positive compact extraction. Therefore r(H)=μ(H)r(H)=\mu(H)r(H)=μ(H) for every such HHH. The reverse implication follows by choosing a compact approximant with positive mass. The construction produces an actual Borel subset in the original space. □\square□

Call a Borel A⊂XA\subset XA⊂X a Radon part of μ\muμ if every Borel E⊂AE\subset AE⊂A is compact inner regular. Equivalently, the measure μA(H)=μ(H∩A)\mu_A(H)=\mu(H\cap A)μA​(H)=μ(H∩A) is a finite Radon measure on XXX. Indeed, apply inner regularity to H∩AH\cap AH∩A to get compacts contained in that actual set; conversely, for E⊂AE\subset AE⊂A, compact approximants for μA(E)\mu_A(E)μA​(E) lie in EEE, where μA=μ\mu_A=\muμA​=μ. Global finiteness supplies local finiteness.

Proposition 3.8 (the largest Radon part). For a finite Borel measure on a locally compact Hausdorff space, the Radon parts form an ideal under Borel subsets and countable unions. Their membership is unchanged by a Borel null modification. There is a Borel Radon part RRR, unique modulo null sets, such that μ(A∖R)=0for every Borel Radon part A.(3.12) \mu(A\setminus R)=0 \quad\text{for every Borel Radon part }A. \tag{3.12} μ(A∖R)=0for every Borel Radon part A.(3.12) The set RRR is a measure carrier, not a claimed closed support.

Proof. Restriction to a Borel subset preserves the defining approximation. If A△BA\triangle BA△B is null and AAA is a Radon part, each Borel E⊂BE\subset BE⊂B has μ(E∩A)=μ(E)\mu(E\cap A)=\mu(E)μ(E∩A)=μ(E). Compact approximants contained in E∩AE\cap AE∩A therefore prove that BBB is also a Radon part.

Suppose AjA_jAj​ are Radon parts and A=⋃jAjA=\bigcup_jA_jA=⋃j​Aj​. For Borel E⊂AE\subset AE⊂A, disjointize the pieces: Ej=E∩(Aj∖⋃i<jAi)E_j=E\cap(A_j\setminus\bigcup_{i<j}A_i)Ej​=E∩(Aj​∖⋃i<j​Ai​). Finiteness chooses NNN such that ∑j>Nμ(Ej)<ε/2\sum_{j>N}\mu(E_j)<\varepsilon/2∑j>N​μ(Ej​)<ε/2. For j≤Nj\le Nj≤N, choose compact Kj⊂EjK_j\subset E_jKj​⊂Ej​ with μ(Ej∖Kj)<ε/(2N)\mu(E_j\setminus K_j)<\varepsilon/(2N)μ(Ej​∖Kj​)<ε/(2N). Their finite union is compact, lies in the actual EEE, and misses mass below ε\varepsilonε. Thus AAA is a Radon part.

Let mmm be the supremum of the masses of all Borel Radon parts. Choose parts AnA_nAn​ whose masses tend to mmm, taking empty sets if m=0m=0m=0, and put R=⋃nAnR=\bigcup_nA_nR=⋃n​An​. By the union assertion, RRR is a Radon part; its mass equals mmm. For any Radon part AAA, the union R∪AR\cup AR∪A is again a part, so μ(R∪A)≤m=μ(R)\mu(R\cup A)\le m=\mu(R)μ(R∪A)≤m=μ(R). This proves (3.12). Applying it in both directions proves uniqueness modulo null sets. □\square□

Lemma 3.9 (transport of a Radon part). Suppose g:X→Xg:X\to Xg:X→X is a homeomorphism and both ggg and g−1g^{-1}g−1 preserve μ\muμ-null sets. Then AAA is a Radon part if and only if gAgAgA is a Radon part.

Proof. The finite measure η(H)=μ(gH)\eta(H)=\mu(gH)η(H)=μ(gH) is absolutely continuous with respect to μ\muμ. We need its uniform finite-measure consequence: for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 there is δ>0\delta>0δ>0 such that μ(H)<δ ⟹ η(H)<ε.(3.13) \mu(H)<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ \eta(H)<\varepsilon. \tag{3.13} μ(H)<δ ⟹ η(H)<ε.(3.13) If this failed, choose HnH_nHn​ with μ(Hn)<2−n\mu(H_n)<2^{-n}μ(Hn​)<2−n and η(Hn)≥ε\eta(H_n)\ge\varepsilonη(Hn​)≥ε. The tail unions Vm=⋃n≥mHnV_m=\bigcup_{n\ge m}H_nVm​=⋃n≥m​Hn​ decrease to a μ\muμ-null set. But η(Vm)≥ε\eta(V_m)\ge\varepsilonη(Vm​)≥ε, so finiteness and continuity from above make their intersection have η\etaη-mass at least ε\varepsilonε, contradicting absolute continuity. This proves (3.13).

For Borel E⊂gAE\subset gAE⊂gA, choose compact C⊂g−1E⊂AC\subset g^{-1}E\subset AC⊂g−1E⊂A with μ(g−1E∖C)<δ\mu(g^{-1}E\setminus C)<\deltaμ(g−1E∖C)<δ. Then gC⊂EgC\subset EgC⊂E is compact in the original topology and μ(E∖gC)=η(g−1E∖C)<ε\mu(E\setminus gC)=\eta(g^{-1}E\setminus C)<\varepsilonμ(E∖gC)=η(g−1E∖C)<ε. Thus gAgAgA is a Radon part. Apply the same argument to g−1g^{-1}g−1 for the converse. Neither invariance of the measure nor a bounded Radon–Nikodym derivative was assumed. □\square□

Theorem 3.10 (ergodic regularity dichotomy). Let GGG act on a locally compact Hausdorff XXX by homeomorphisms, preserving the null sets of a nonzero finite Borel measure μ\muμ. Suppose the measure-algebra action is ergodic: a Borel BBB with μ(gB△B)=0\mu(gB\triangle B)=0μ(gB△B)=0 for every ggg is null or conull. Then exactly one of the following holds:

  1. μ\muμ is Radon on the original XXX.
  2. Every positive Borel E⊂XE\subset XE⊂X contains a positive Borel F⊂EF\subset EF⊂E for which every compact C⊂FC\subset FC⊂F has measure zero.

Moreover, one positive Borel Radon part suffices for the first alternative. Under the chapter's jointly Borel standard-measure action convention, exactly invariant-set ergodicity suffices: Free actions and the crossed-product diagonal, Proposition 4.7, proves the required invariant-class equivalence for a separable locally compact group.

Proof. Take the maximal Radon part RRR from Proposition 3.8. Lemma 3.9 makes gRgRgR a Radon part, so μ(gR∖R)=0\mu(gR\setminus R)=0μ(gR∖R)=0. Applying this to g−1g^{-1}g−1, and then transporting its null exceptional set by ggg, gives μ(R∖gR)=0\mu(R\setminus gR)=0μ(R∖gR)=0. Therefore μ(gR△R)=0(g∈G).(3.14) \mu(gR\triangle R)=0\qquad(g\in G). \tag{3.14} μ(gR△R)=0(g∈G).(3.14) This is invariance of one measure class for every fixed ggg; no intersection of uncountably many conull sets is taken. Ergodicity makes RRR null or conull.

If RRR is conull, the null-modification assertion of Proposition 3.8 makes XXX itself a Radon part. Hence μ\muμ is Radon. Any positive Radon part forces μ(R)>0\mu(R)>0μ(R)>0, so forces this case.

If RRR is null, no positive Borel set is a Radon part. Given positive EEE, there is therefore a Borel H⊂EH\subset EH⊂E with r(H)<μ(H)r(H)<\mu(H)r(H)<μ(H). Lemma 3.7 supplies the positive Borel F⊂H⊂EF\subset H\subset EF⊂H⊂E in alternative 2. The alternatives are disjoint because Radon regularity would give a positive compact subset of this FFF. □\square□

Corollary 3.11 (the exact compact-extraction question). In the finite, pointwise free source setting, fix any g≠eg\ne eg=e. The assertion for every positive Borel E, ∃ L⊂E compact:μ(L)>0,gL∩L=∅(3.15) \text{for every positive Borel }E,\ \exists\,L\subset E\text{ compact}: \mu(L)>0,\quad gL\cap L=\varnothing \tag{3.15} for every positive Borel E, ∃L⊂E compact:μ(L)>0,gL∩L=∅(3.15) is equivalent to μ\muμ being Radon in the original topology. If the action is ergodic in Theorem 3.10's sense, it is enough to prove (3.15) for all positive Borel subsets of one positive Borel part AAA.

Proof. Assertion (3.15) supplies positive compact extraction after forgetting the disjointness condition. Lemma 3.7 with E=XE=XE=X proves compact inner regularity on all Borel sets. Conversely, the original one-element separation and finite-cover proof in Compact fixed sets and free Polish models, Lemma 2.1, gives (3.15) for a finite Radon measure. For the localized assertion, Lemma 3.7 makes AAA a positive Radon part, and Theorem 3.10 makes μ\muμ Radon everywhere. The quantifier ranges over every positive Borel subset; one positive compact set alone does not suffice. □\square□

Corollary 3.12 (the possible atomless obstruction). Retain the full source setting and its standing jointly Borel standard-measure convention. If the second alternative of Theorem 3.10 occurs, then μ\muμ is atomless. For every positive Borel EEE and every compact K⊂G∖{e}K\subset G\setminus\{e\}K⊂G∖{e}, there is a positive Borel F⊂EF\subset EF⊂E such that F∩kF=∅(k∈K),μ(C)=0(C⊂F compact).(3.16) F\cap kF=\varnothing\quad(k\in K),\qquad \mu(C)=0\quad(C\subset F\text{ compact}). \tag{3.16} F∩kF=∅(k∈K),μ(C)=0(C⊂F compact).(3.16)

Proof. A positive measure atom would, by Lemma 3.4, give a positive singleton. That singleton is a positive Radon part, contradicting the second alternative. Thus the measure is atomless.

Theorem 3.10 first gives a positive Borel H⊂EH\subset EH⊂E with no positive compact subset. Apply the complete measurable wandering proof, Theorem 3.2, to HHH and the prescribed KKK. It supplies a positive Borel F⊂HF\subset HF⊂H missing all its kkk-translates at once. Every compact subset of FFF is a compact subset of HHH, hence null. This proves (3.16). The statement is conditional on alternative 2 occurring; no example satisfying all the standing standard-measure dynamical hypotheses is asserted. □\square□

These reductions identify the remaining source decision precisely: do the full standing atomless standard-measure, free, ergodic, quasi-invariant, full-support hypotheses force the first alternative? A measure-only nonregular example does not answer that question. A compact conull carrier, or even a positive compact set, does not supply a Radon restriction on that carrier.

Lemma 3.13 (support and nonsingular transport). For a finite Borel measure on a Hausdorff space, define Sμ={x:μ(U)>0 for every open U∋x}.(3.17) S_\mu=\{x:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every open }U\ni x\}. \tag{3.17} Sμ​={x:μ(U)>0 for every open U∋x}.(3.17) This set is closed. If XXX is compact and μ(X)>0\mu(X)>0μ(X)>0, it is nonempty. Equivalent Borel measures have the same support. If h:X→Xh:X\to Xh:X→X is a homeomorphism, then Sh∗μ=hSμS_{h_*\mu}=hS_\muSh∗​μ​=hSμ​. In particular every nonsingular homeomorphism preserves SμS_\muSμ​ exactly.

Proof. The complement of SμS_\muSμ​ is the union of all open sets of measure zero, and is therefore open. If the support were empty on a compact XXX, those zero-measure open sets would cover XXX; a finite subcover would force μ(X)=0\mu(X)=0μ(X)=0. Equivalence of measures gives the same collection of zero-measure open sets. An open neighborhood UUU of hxhxhx has h−1Uh^{-1}Uh−1U as an open neighborhood of xxx, and (h∗μ)(U)=μ(h−1U)(h_*\mu)(U)=\mu(h^{-1}U)(h∗​μ)(U)=μ(h−1U). This proves the transport formula. Combining it with equivalence proves exact invariance. No uncountable intersection of conull sets is involved. □\square□

Nonemptiness of the support has not asserted that it carries any mass. The next proposition gives a precise test for that failure.

Proposition 3.14 (a locally countable conull carrier has null support). Let XXX be compact Hausdorff, μ\muμ a Borel probability with μ({x})=0\mu(\{x\})=0μ({x})=0 for every xxx, D⊂XD\subset XD⊂X closed, and Y⊂DY\subset DY⊂D Borel with μ(Y)=1\mu(Y)=1μ(Y)=1. Suppose that for every y∈Yy\in Yy∈Y there is an ambient open neighborhood UyU_yUy​ such that Uy∩DU_y\cap DUy​∩D is countable. Then ∅≠Sμ⊂D∖Y,μ(Sμ)=0,μ(X∖Sμ)=1.(3.18) \varnothing\ne S_\mu\subset D\setminus Y,\qquad \mu(S_\mu)=0,\qquad \mu(X\setminus S_\mu)=1. \tag{3.18} ∅=Sμ​⊂D∖Y,μ(Sμ​)=0,μ(X∖Sμ​)=1.(3.18) The open set X∖SμX\setminus S_\muX∖Sμ​ is a union of zero-measure open sets but has measure one. Every compact subset of YYY is countable and null.

Proof. Since YYY is conull, μ(X∖D)=0\mu(X\setminus D)=0μ(X∖D)=0. Countable additivity and the singleton hypothesis give μ(Uy∩D)=0\mu(U_y\cap D)=0μ(Uy​∩D)=0; hence μ(Uy)=0\mu(U_y)=0μ(Uy​)=0. Thus no y∈Yy\in Yy∈Y belongs to the support. No point outside the closed set DDD belongs to it either, since X∖DX\setminus DX∖D is a zero-measure open neighborhood. This proves Sμ⊂D∖YS_\mu\subset D\setminus YSμ​⊂D∖Y. Lemma 3.13 supplies nonemptiness and closedness, and the displayed containment gives its zero mass.

By the definition of support, X∖SμX\setminus S_\muX∖Sμ​ is the union of the zero-measure open neighborhoods just described, including any others. It is Borel and has measure one. Countable additivity makes every countable subunion null; it does not make this arbitrary union null.

If C⊂YC\subset YC⊂Y is compact, the UyU_yUy​'s cover CCC. Finitely many suffice, and CCC is contained in their finite union of countable intersections with DDD. Therefore CCC is countable and has measure zero. □\square□

Corollary 3.15 (the two proposed repairs). Under Proposition 3.14's hypotheses, replacing μ\muμ by any equivalent finite measure leaves the support unchanged and null. Restricting μ\muμ to its support gives the zero measure. Suppose additionally that XXX has a countable dense subset Q={qn:n≥1}Q=\{q_n:n\ge1\}Q={qn​:n≥1} of distinct points. Choose cn>0c_n>0cn​>0 with ∑ncn=1\sum_n c_n=1∑n​cn​=1, set η=∑ncnδqn\eta=\sum_n c_n\delta_{q_n}η=∑n​cn​δqn​​, and fix 0<t<10<t<10<t<1. The probability λ=(1−t)μ+tη(3.19) \lambda=(1-t)\mu+t\eta \tag{3.19} λ=(1−t)μ+tη(3.19) has full support, but cannot be ergodic under any group of nonsingular homeomorphisms. It still has a positive Borel subset with no positive compact subset.

Proof. Lemma 3.13 proves the equivalent-measure assertion; equivalence also preserves the nullity of SμS_\muSμ​. Its restriction is zero because every Borel subset of it is null.

Every nonempty open set meets QQQ, so its λ\lambdaλ-measure is positive. The set of positive point masses of λ\lambdaλ is exactly QQQ, and λ(Q)=t\lambda(Q)=tλ(Q)=t. A nonsingular bijection preserves the property that a singleton is null and hence permutes QQQ. Thus QQQ is an exactly invariant Borel set of intermediate measure for every proposed nonsingular action. This contradicts ergodicity.

Finally Y∖QY\setminus QY∖Q is Borel with λ(Y∖Q)=1−t\lambda(Y\setminus Q)=1-tλ(Y∖Q)=1−t. Every compact C⊂Y∖QC\subset Y\setminus QC⊂Y∖Q is countable by Proposition 3.14, has μ(C)=0\mu(C)=0μ(C)=0, and misses the atomic measure's carrier. Therefore λ(C)=0\lambda(C)=0λ(C)=0. This proves the last assertion in the actual original topology. □\square□

Primary-source comparison. Wage's CH construction uses I=[0,1]I=[0,1]I=[0,1] and X0=I×{0,1}X_0=I\times\{0,1\}X0​=I×{0,1}; write ai=(a,i)a^i=(a,i)ai=(a,i). In Z=(X0,σ)×(X0,τ)Z=(X_0,\sigma)\times(X_0,\tau)Z=(X0​,σ)×(X0​,τ), the double diagonal D={(ai,aj):a∈I, i,j∈{0,1}}D=\{(a^i,a^j):a\in I,\ i,j\in\{0,1\}\}D={(ai,aj):a∈I, i,j∈{0,1}} is closed and Y={(a1,a1):a∈I}Y=\{(a^1,a^1):a\in I\}Y={(a1,a1):a∈I}. This is a comparison of those properties, not an import of the transfinite construction or a counterexample to all the source dynamical hypotheses.

Atomless orbit mixtures: support can be repaired while returns decide ergodicity

The dense-atomic repair in Corollary 3.15 is not the only way to supply full support. One can instead sum translates of an atomless measure. The following results prove what this operation preserves and identify its exact ergodicity requirement. They are conditional on the specified seed and action; no omitted part of Wage's construction is assumed proved here.

Let a countable group GGG act on a compact Hausdorff space XXX by homeomorphisms. The group has the discrete topology, so this is a jointly continuous action. Let ν\nuν be a Borel probability, choose cg>0c_g>0cg​>0 with ∑g∈Gcg=1\sum_{g\in G}c_g=1∑g∈G​cg​=1, and define νg(B)=ν(g−1B),μ(B)=∑g∈Gcgνg(B),[B]G=⋃g∈GgB.(3.20) \nu_g(B)=\nu(g^{-1}B),\qquad \mu(B)=\sum_{g\in G}c_g\nu_g(B),\qquad [B]_G=\bigcup_{g\in G}gB. \tag{3.20} νg​(B)=ν(g−1B),μ(B)=g∈G∑​cg​νg​(B),[B]G​=g∈G⋃​gB.(3.20) All saturations in this subsection are countable unions of Borel sets. We write S(η)=supp⁡XηS(\eta)=\operatorname{supp}_X\etaS(η)=suppX​η for the original-topology support of a measure.

Lemma 3.16 (null ideal and support of an orbit mixture). Formula (3.20) defines a quasi-invariant Borel probability, and for every Borel BBB μ(B)=0 ⟺ ν(g−1B)=0 for every g∈G ⟺ ν([B]G)=0.(3.21) \mu(B)=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \nu(g^{-1}B)=0\text{ for every }g\in G \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \nu([B]_G)=0. \tag{3.21} μ(B)=0 ⟺ ν(g−1B)=0 for every g∈G ⟺ ν([B]G​)=0.(3.21) Its support is S(μ)=⋃g∈GgS(ν)‾.(3.22) S(\mu)=\overline{\bigcup_{g\in G}gS(\nu)}. \tag{3.22} S(μ)=g∈G⋃​gS(ν)​.(3.22) In particular a minimal action, meaning that every orbit is dense, makes μ\muμ fully supported.

Proof. Each νg\nu_gνg​ is a Borel probability. Interchanging two sums of nonnegative numbers proves countable additivity of μ\muμ; its total mass is ∑gcg=1\sum_gc_g=1∑g​cg​=1. Positivity of all weights proves the first equivalence in (3.21). A countable union has zero ν\nuν-measure exactly when each of its members does. Inversion permutes the group indices, proving the second equivalence.

For h∈Gh\in Gh∈G, νg(hB)=νh−1g(B).(3.23) \nu_g(hB)=\nu_{h^{-1}g}(B). \tag{3.23} νg​(hB)=νh−1g​(B).(3.23) Thus the first criterion in (3.21) is unchanged by B↦hBB\mapsto hBB↦hB. Applying this also to h−1h^{-1}h−1 proves quasi-invariance. This does not assert that ν\nuν itself is quasi-invariant.

Put F=⋃ggS(ν)‾F=\overline{\bigcup_g gS(\nu)}F=⋃g​gS(ν)​. If x∈Fx\in Fx∈F, each neighborhood of xxx contains a point of gS(ν)gS(\nu)gS(ν) for some ggg. That open neighborhood has positive νg\nu_gνg​-measure and hence positive μ\muμ-measure. Thus F⊂S(μ)F\subset S(\mu)F⊂S(μ). Conversely, if x∉Fx\notin Fx∈/F, a compact neighborhood CCC of xxx can be chosen inside X∖FX\setminus FX∖F. For each fixed ggg, every point of CCC lies outside S(νg)=gS(ν)S(\nu_g)=gS(\nu)S(νg​)=gS(ν), so a finite cover by νg\nu_gνg​-null open sets gives νg(C)=0\nu_g(C)=0νg​(C)=0. A positive open set need not meet the support of a nonregular measure: Proposition 3.14 supplies exactly such a conull open set. Formula (3.22) follows by compact neighborhoods outside the closure, and does not use that false inference.

Lemma 3.17 (strong standardness and atomlessness survive). Suppose Y⊂XY\subset XY⊂X is Borel, ν(Y)=1\nu(Y)=1ν(Y)=1, and its relative Borel sigma-algebra makes it a standard Borel space. The exact return condition is deliberate. A seed-null set can have a positive saturation when the seed itself is not quasi-invariant. Exactifying invariance using ν\nuν-null sets alone would therefore be invalid. The countable exactification above uses the already quasi-invariant mixture μ\muμ. Equation (3.21) specifies the null ideal which is safe to saturate.

Figure 5. This symbolic diagram describes Proposition 3.20, conditional on its explicitly specified compact torus seed. Distinct levels are the exact coordinates nα∗+Zn\alpha_*+\mathbb Znα∗​+Z, not parallel Euclidean copies of the whole product. The weights are 2−∣n∣/32^{-|n|}/32−∣n∣/3. Every compact subset of the conull standard carrier has zero mass, while saturation of an intermediate seed event keeps its exact mass and prevents ergodicity. Lemmas 3.16–3.17 prove full support and strong standardness; Proposition 3.18 proves persistence of pure nonregularity; Theorem 3.19 identifies the exact return condition. Wage's reported Borel diagonal properties motivate the seed search, but neither an unproved embedding of that construction nor its omitted induction is imported. Proposition 3.20 alone does not give the standing ergodic source hypotheses; Theorem 3.29 below realizes them under CH after verifying the finite-power Borel gate.

A Bernoulli repair with an explicit product-Borel condition

Proposition 3.20 repairs support and pointwise freeness, but retains invariant events from its seed. The following construction repairs ergodicity too, provided a further measurable-topological condition is verified. The condition concerns the inherited topology, not a new Polish topology chosen to represent the same measure space.

Lemma 3.21 (finite powers control the countable product). Let YYY be a topological space, let B(Y)\mathcal B(Y)B(Y) be its actual Borel sigma-algebra, and suppose for every positive integer rrr that B(Yr)=B(Y)⊗r.(3.35) \mathcal B(Y^r)=\mathcal B(Y)^{\otimes r}. \tag{3.35} B(Yr)=B(Y)⊗r.(3.35) Then, for the product topologies, B(YZ)=B(Y)⊗Z,(3.36) \mathcal B(Y^{\mathbb Z}) =\mathcal B(Y)^{\otimes\mathbb Z}, \tag{3.36} B(YZ)=B(Y)⊗Z,(3.36) and B(YZ×T)=B(Y)⊗Z⊗B(T).(3.37) \mathcal B(Y^{\mathbb Z}\times\mathbb T) =\mathcal B(Y)^{\otimes\mathbb Z} \otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb T). \tag{3.37} B(YZ×T)=B(Y)⊗Z⊗B(T).(3.37)

Proof. Coordinate projections are continuous, so the sigma-algebra on the right of (3.36) is contained in the one on the left. For the reverse inclusion, let U⊂YZU\subset Y^{\mathbb Z}U⊂YZ be open. For each finite F⊂ZF\subset\mathbb ZF⊂Z, let OF⊂YFO_F\subset Y^FOF​⊂YF be the union of all open V⊂YFV\subset Y^FV⊂YF for which πF−1(V)⊂U\pi_F^{-1}(V)\subset UπF−1​(V)⊂U. Basic product neighborhoods give U=⋃F⊂Z, F finiteπF−1(OF).(3.38) U=\bigcup_{F\subset\mathbb Z,\ F\ {\rm finite}} \pi_F^{-1}(O_F). \tag{3.38} U=F⊂Z, F finite⋃​πF−1​(OF​).(3.38) There are only countably many finite FFF. Each OFO_FOF​ is open in a finite power and is product-Borel by (3.35); ordering FFF identifies it with the corresponding YrY^rYr. The empty set of coordinates just permits the empty set or the whole space. Thus (3.38) is product-measurable.

For the circle factor, fix a countable base J\mathcal JJ of open arcs. Given open U⊂YZ×TU\subset Y^{\mathbb Z}\times\mathbb TU⊂YZ×T, let OF,JO_{F,J}OF,J​ be the union of all open V⊂YFV\subset Y^FV⊂YF with πF−1(V)×J⊂U\pi_F^{-1}(V)\times J\subset UπF−1​(V)×J⊂U. The countable union of these products over finite FFF and J∈JJ\in\mathcal JJ∈J equals UUU. Condition (3.35) again makes every member measurable. Continuous coordinate projections prove the other inclusion in (3.37). No countable base for YYY has been assumed. □\square□

Lemma 3.22 (the Bernoulli probability and its eigenfunctions). Let (Y,η)(Y,\eta)(Y,η) be a standard Borel probability space. There is a unique probability ηZ\eta^{\mathbb Z}ηZ on its countable product sigma-algebra with independent coordinates of law η\etaη. The shift (σy)j=yj+1(3.39) (\sigma y)_j=y_{j+1} \tag{3.39} (σy)j​=yj+1​(3.39) preserves it and is mixing. Its only L2L^2L2 eigenfunctions with eigenvalue of absolute value one are constants, with eigenvalue one.

Proof. We describe the probability construction to keep the needed independence explicit. Use the classical standard Borel representation input to identify YYY measurably with a Borel subset B⊂[0,1]B\subset[0,1]B⊂[0,1]. This identification concerns sigma-algebras and makes no assertion about YYY's given topology. Push η\etaη to a Borel probability θ\thetaθ on [0,1][0,1][0,1]. Its distribution function H(t)=θ([0,t])H(t)=\theta([0,t])H(t)=θ([0,t]) is increasing and right-continuous. For 0<u<10<u<10<u<1, set q(u)=inf⁡{t∈[0,1]:H(t)≥u}q(u)=\inf\{t\in[0,1]:H(t)\ge u\}q(u)=inf{t∈[0,1]:H(t)≥u}. Right continuity gives q(u)≤t⟺u≤H(t),0≤t≤1.(3.40) q(u)\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\le H(t), \qquad 0\le t\le1. \tag{3.40} q(u)≤t⟺u≤H(t),0≤t≤1.(3.40) Consequently qqq is Borel and sends ordinary length probability to θ\thetaθ: the interval probabilities agree, and the pi-lambda theorem extends agreement to all Borel sets. Since θ(B)=1\theta(B)=1θ(B)=1, replace the values outside BBB, and the endpoint values, by a fixed point of BBB. Compose with the inverse representation to obtain a measurable sampling map into YYY of law η\etaη.

The binary digits of length probability on [0,1)[0,1)[0,1) are independent fair bits. Indeed a prescription of finitely many digit positions is a union of equal-length dyadic half-open intervals and has probability 2−m2^{-m}2−m when mmm digits are prescribed. Use the terminating expansion at dyadic points, a null set. Partition the digit positions into countably many disjoint infinite sets indexed by Z\mathbb ZZ. The binary numbers formed from each set are uniform on [0,1][0,1][0,1] and are independent: dyadic interval events use finitely many disjoint digit positions, and the pi-lambda theorem extends their joint probabilities to Borel rectangles. Apply the sampling map to these numbers. The resulting measurable map into YZY^{\mathbb Z}YZ pushes length to the asserted probability. Finite-coordinate rectangles determine it uniquely by the pi-lambda theorem. They also show that coordinate permutation, in particular σ\sigmaσ, preserves it. An extra independent set of digits gives an independent circle coordinate when needed below.

Bounded finite-coordinate functions are dense in L2(ηZ)L^2(\eta^{\mathbb Z})L2(ηZ). To prove this, the class of events whose indicators can be approximated by such functions in L2L^2L2 is a lambda-system containing the finite-cylinder pi-system. Complements preserve approximability. For a disjoint countable union first truncate it to finitely many events; the squared indicator error is the probability of the omitted tail, which tends to zero. Finite sums of approximants finish the argument. The pi-lambda theorem and approximation of measurable functions by simple functions prove density.

If bounded fff and ggg depend on finite coordinate sets FFF and JJJ, then f∘σnf\circ\sigma^nf∘σn and ggg depend on disjoint sets for all sufficiently large positive nnn. Independence gives exact factorization then. Density, invariance and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore give, for arbitrary f,g∈L2f,g\in L^2f,g∈L2, ∫(f∘σn)g‾ dηZ⟶(∫f dηZ)(∫g dηZ)‾.(3.41) \int (f\circ\sigma^n)\overline g\,d\eta^{\mathbb Z} \longrightarrow \left(\int f\,d\eta^{\mathbb Z}\right) \overline{\left(\int g\,d\eta^{\mathbb Z}\right)}. \tag{3.41} ∫(f∘σn)g​dηZ⟶(∫fdηZ)(∫gdηZ)​.(3.41) This is mixing.

Suppose f∘σ=ζff\circ\sigma=\zeta ff∘σ=ζf, ∣ζ∣=1|\zeta|=1∣ζ∣=1. Integration forces ∫f=0\int f=0∫f=0 if ζ≠1\zeta\ne1ζ=1. When ζ=1\zeta=1ζ=1, subtract the mean. For the resulting mean-zero eigenfunction hhh, the left side of (3.41), with f=g=hf=g=hf=g=h, is ζn∥h∥22\zeta^n\|h\|_2^2ζn∥h∥22​, whereas its limit must be zero. Its absolute value is constant, so h=0h=0h=0. The asserted eigenfunction conclusion follows. □\square□

Theorem 3.23 (conditional ergodic repair of a compact-extraction seed). Suppose:

  • KKK is separable compact Hausdorff;
  • ν\nuν is a fully supported Borel probability on KKK;
  • Y⊂KY\subset KY⊂K is a conull Borel subset whose actual relative Borel space is standard Borel;
  • every compact C⊂YC\subset YC⊂Y satisfies ν(C)=0\nu(C)=0ν(C)=0;
  • the finite-power condition (3.35) holds for the topology inherited by YYY from KKK.

Then there is a separable compact Hausdorff XXX, a jointly continuous pointwise free Z\mathbb ZZ-action on XXX, and a fully supported, invariant, ergodic, atomless Borel probability μ\muμ, standard on an actual conull Borel subspace E⊂XE\subset XE⊂X, such that μ(E)=1,L⊂E compact ⟹ μ(L)=0.(3.42) \begin{gathered} \mu(E)=1,\\ L\subset E\ {\rm compact}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu(L)=0. \end{gathered} \tag{3.42} μ(E)=1,L⊂E compact ⟹ μ(L)=0.​(3.42) Thus an actual seed satisfying all five hypotheses would refute positive compact extraction at the remaining atomless standard-measure interpretation of source Exercise 5(a).

Proof. Let η\etaη be the restriction of ν\nuν to the relative Borel sigma-algebra on YYY, and let ℓ\ellℓ be circle length probability. Choose an irrational α∈R\alpha\in\mathbb Rα∈R and put X=KZ×T,E=YZ×T,(3.43) X=K^{\mathbb Z}\times\mathbb T,\qquad E=Y^{\mathbb Z}\times\mathbb T, \tag{3.43} X=KZ×T,E=YZ×T,(3.43) T(x,z)=(σx,z+α+Z).(3.44) T(x,z)=(\sigma x,z+\alpha+\mathbb Z). \tag{3.44} T(x,z)=(σx,z+α+Z).(3.44) The ultrafilter compactness proof in Separable compact actions with nonregular measures, Section 1, applies verbatim with compact KKK in each integer coordinate and the circle in the last coordinate: each projected ultrafilter has a limit, and finitely many coordinate neighborhoods prove product convergence. Distinct coordinates separate distinct points. Hence XXX is compact Hausdorff. If D⊂KD\subset KD⊂K is countable dense and d0∈Dd_0\in Dd0​∈D, sequences taking values in DDD and equal to d0d_0d0​ outside a finite set form a countable dense subset of KZK^{\mathbb Z}KZ. Pairing them with rational circle points proves separability, using precisely the finite-coordinate basis. The shift and rotation are homeomorphisms. Their integer powers define a jointly continuous action since Z\mathbb ZZ is discrete.

The set EEE is ambient Borel, being the intersection of the countably many coordinate conditions xj∈Yx_j\in Yxj​∈Y. Borel sigma-algebras of subspaces are traces of ambient Borel sigma-algebras: both inclusions follow respectively from continuous inclusion and from writing relative open sets as intersections with ambient open sets. Lemma 3.21 thus makes the inclusion ι:(YZ×T, B(Y)⊗Z⊗B(T))⟶X(3.45) \iota: (Y^{\mathbb Z}\times\mathbb T,\ \mathcal B(Y)^{\otimes\mathbb Z} \otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb T)) \longrightarrow X \tag{3.45} ι:(YZ×T, B(Y)⊗Z⊗B(T))⟶X(3.45) measurable, and identifies its domain sigma-algebra exactly with the relative Borel sigma-algebra on EEE. Define μ=ι∗(ηZ⊗ℓ).(3.46) \mu=\iota_*(\eta^{\mathbb Z}\otimes\ell). \tag{3.46} μ=ι∗​(ηZ⊗ℓ).(3.46) The product probability is supplied by Lemma 3.22, including its extra independent coordinate. Countable products of standard Borel spaces are standard Borel: represent YYY as a Borel subset of a Polish space, take the countable product of that space, and note that the product subset is a countable intersection of coordinate inverse images of Borel sets. Its product Borel sigma-algebra is the coordinate sigma-algebra because a countable product of second countable spaces has a countable base. This proves actual strong standardness of EEE under (3.37), rather than merely separability of its measure algebra. Also μ(E)=1\mu(E)=1μ(E)=1.

Shift invariance and circle translation invariance prove T∗μ=μT_*\mu=\muT∗​μ=μ, hence quasi-invariance. Every nonempty basic open cylinder in XXX has mass μ(⋂j∈Fπj−1(Uj)∩πT−1(J))=ℓ(J)∏j∈Fν(Uj)>0(3.47) \begin{gathered} \mu\left(\bigcap_{j\in F}\pi_j^{-1}(U_j) \cap\pi_{\mathbb T}^{-1}(J)\right)\\ =\ell(J)\prod_{j\in F}\nu(U_j)>0 \end{gathered} \tag{3.47} μ​j∈F⋂​πj−1​(Uj​)∩πT−1​(J)​=ℓ(J)j∈F∏​ν(Uj​)>0​(3.47) when the UjU_jUj​ are nonempty open subsets of KKK and JJJ is a nonempty open circle arc. Here conullness gives η(Uj∩Y)=ν(Uj)\eta(U_j\cap Y)=\nu(U_j)η(Uj​∩Y)=ν(Uj​). Every nonempty open set contains such a cylinder, proving full support. A singleton has measure zero since its circle coordinate is a singleton of zero length. Lemma 3.4 on the conull standard carrier proves atomlessness.

Realizing the whole seed under the continuum hypothesis

Theorem 3.23 has an actual realization if the continuum hypothesis (CH) is assumed: 2ℵ0=ℵ12^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_12ℵ0​=ℵ1​. We keep that extra set-theoretic hypothesis throughout this subsection. It is not inferred from the source exercise. The construction retains the actual inherited topologies and proves the finite-power Borel equalities, rather than merely extending probabilities to completions.

The recursive topological method is related to de la Vega and Kunen's Theorem 2.4, Section 2, pages 2–3. We give the successor construction explicitly, prove the hereditary-separability induction with the global mixed topology, and then prove the additional finite-power Borel result needed here. Their later homogeneity theorems are not used.

  • τ\tauτ is first countable and has a basis of countable compact clopen sets;
  • the following requirement holds. If S⊂CnS\subset C^nS⊂Cn is countable, then, after some countable ordinal bound depending on SSS, every tuple whose last coordinate has strictly larger ordinal index than all its other coordinates satisfies f∈S‾ τn−1×ρ⟹f∈S‾ τn.(3.53) f\in\overline S^{\,\tau^{n-1}\times\rho} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f\in\overline S^{\,\tau^n}. \tag{3.53} f∈Sτn−1×ρ⟹f∈Sτn.(3.53) For n=1n=1n=1, the mixed topology in (3.53) is just ρ\rhoρ.

Proof. Identify CCC with ω1\omega_1ω1​ using CH, but retain ρ\rhoρ as a topology on those points. There are only ℵ1\aleph_1ℵ1​ countable subsets of all the finite powers combined: ∣⋃n≥1[Cn]≤ℵ0∣≤ℵ0(2ℵ0)ℵ0=ℵ1.(3.54) \left|\bigcup_{n\ge1}[C^n]^{\le\aleph_0}\right| \le\aleph_0(2^{\aleph_0})^{\aleph_0} =\aleph_1. \tag{3.54} ​n≥1⋃​[Cn]≤ℵ0​​≤ℵ0​(2ℵ0​)ℵ0​=ℵ1​.(3.54) List them as (Sμ,nμ)(S_\mu,n_\mu)(Sμ​,nμ​), allowing harmless repetitions, and arrange Sμ⊂μ nμ.(3.55) S_\mu\subset\mu^{\,n_\mu}. \tag{3.55} Sμ​⊂μnμ​.(3.55) Here is the indexing justification. First list the requirements with ω1\omega_1ω1​ indices. Recursively assign each one a larger still-unused countable ordinal than all its coordinate indices and all previously assigned indices. At a countable stage their supremum is countable, so such an ordinal exists. Fill unused indices with the empty subset of the one-fold power. Thus every requirement is assigned, with (3.55).

Construct topologies on open initial segments by induction. At a limit stage, take the topology generated by the earlier open-segment topologies. At a successor stage adding ξ\xiξ, the old initial segment ξ\xiξ is countable. Its first countable topology has a countable base, obtained by taking the union of countable local bases over its countably many points.

For every μ<ξ\mu<\xiμ<ξ with nμ=nn_\mu=nnμ​=n, and every basic product-open UUU in the first n−1n-1n−1 old coordinates, form the countable set Aμ,U=πn(Sμ∩(U×ξ))⊂ξ.(3.56) A_{\mu,U} =\pi_n\bigl(S_\mu\cap(U\times\xi)\bigr)\subset\xi. \tag{3.56} Aμ,U​=πn​(Sμ​∩(U×ξ))⊂ξ.(3.56) For n=1n=1n=1 use Aμ,U=SμA_{\mu,U}=S_\muAμ,U​=Sμ​. Among these countably many sets impose precisely those with ξ∈Aμ,U‾ ρ\xi\in\overline{A_{\mu,U}}^{\,\rho}ξ∈Aμ,U​​ρ. Lemma 3.24, with the ordinary Cantor coordinates as the injection, supplies the new compact-clopen neighborhood basis and all the required accumulations. If none accumulate, its isolated-point case applies. Old topology, compactness of old basic neighborhoods and their clopen property are preserved at each step.

The limit steps preserve these properties too: each point belongs to an earlier open segment, whose compact-clopen basic neighborhoods still retain their exact subspace topology. They remain compact and open in the final Hausdorff space, hence closed. The ordinary Cantor topology is contained in the final topology because every ordinary open set restricts to an old open set on each initial segment, and is the union of these restrictions. It also supplies Hausdorff separation globally. Every new neighborhood in (3.52) is contained in the countable segment ξ+1\xi+1ξ+1, proving that every such compact-clopen basic neighborhood is countable.

To prove (3.53), take the index μ\muμ of SSS and a tuple fff whose last ordinal coordinate ξ\xiξ exceeds μ\muμ and all its other coordinates. Every full product neighborhood of fff contains U×WU\times WU×W where UUU is an old product-basic neighborhood of the first n−1n-1n−1 coordinates and WWW is a new neighborhood of ξ\xiξ. Mixed closure says that every ordinary neighborhood of ξ\xiξ meets (3.56). The requirement at stage ξ\xiξ therefore says that WWW meets (3.56). A witnessing tuple in S∩(U×W)S\cap(U\times W)S∩(U×W) proves full product closure. Initial-segment coherence ensures these neighborhoods retain their meaning in the final topology. □\square□

Lemma 3.26 (all finite powers are hereditarily separable). Every subspace of (C,τ)n(C,\tau)^n(C,τ)n, for n≥1n\ge1n≥1, is separable.

Proof. First, if every subspace of AAA is separable and BBB has a countable base (Vj)(V_j)(Vj​), every subspace D⊂A×BD\subset A\times BD⊂A×B is separable. For each jjj, project D∩(A×Vj)D\cap(A\times V_j)D∩(A×Vj​) onto AAA, choose a countable dense subset of that projection, and choose one witness in D∩(A×Vj)D\cap(A\times V_j)D∩(A×Vj​) over each chosen point. The union of the witnesses is countable. Given a nonempty relative basic rectangle in DDD, choose VjV_jVj​ inside its second-coordinate neighborhood and containing a witnessing second coordinate. Density in that projection then supplies a chosen witness in the rectangle. This proves the assertion with no measurable-selection claim.

Induct on nnn. For a subspace D⊂CnD\subset C^nD⊂Cn, the portions where two coordinates agree are homeomorphic to subspaces of a smaller power, and are separable by induction. The distinct-coordinate portion is a finite union of subspaces obtained by specifying the ordinal order of its coordinates. Coordinate permutations reduce each one to the case of strictly increasing coordinates. This is a partition of sets for a topological separability proof; it makes no assertion that the ordinal-order relation is Borel.

Fix one increasing-coordinate portion after permuting its coordinates, and denote that portion again by DDD. The induction hypothesis and the preceding product argument show that the global mixed space (C,τ)n−1×(C,ρ)(C,\tau)^{n-1}\times(C,\rho)(C,τ)n−1×(C,ρ) is hereditarily separable. Choose a countable subset S⊂DS\subset DS⊂D dense in that mixed topology. For n=1n=1n=1, ordinary second countability supplies this subset directly. Let μ\muμ be its enumeration index in Lemma 3.25. Every increasing tuple of DDD whose largest coordinate ξ\xiξ exceeds μ\muμ is in the full τn\tau^nτn closure of SSS, by (3.53). The remaining tuples lie in the countable set (μ+1)n(\mu+1)^n(μ+1)n. Adjoining those members of DDD to SSS gives a countable full-topology dense subset. Combining the finitely many portions proves the claim. □\square□

Proposition 3.28 (the complete seed list is realized under CH). Assume CH. There exist a separable compact Hausdorff KKK, a fully supported Borel probability ν\nuν on it, and an actual conull Borel standard subspace V⊂KV\subset KV⊂K, such that every compact subset of VVV is ν\nuν-null and every finite power of VVV satisfies (3.35).

Proof. Write Y=(C,τ)Y=(C,\tau)Y=(C,τ). Every compact subset of YYY is countable: cover it by countable compact-open basic neighborhoods and take a finite subcover. Give its actual Borel sigma-algebra the ordinary fair-coin Cantor probability η\etaη, which is available on that sigma-algebra by (3.57). Lemma 3.22 constructs the independent coin probability; the ordinary countable cylinder base identifies its sigma-algebra with the Cantor Borel sigma-algebra. Singletons are null since each prescribed first mmm digits has mass 2−m2^{-m}2−m. Thus every compact subset of YYY is null, and YYY is an actual standard Borel probability space.

Let D=Y⊔{∞}D=Y\sqcup\{\infty\}D=Y⊔{∞} be its one-point compactification: old open sets remain open, and neighborhoods of ∞\infty∞ are complements of compact subsets of YYY. These form a topology because compact subsets are closed in Hausdorff YYY, finite unions of compact sets are compact, and a closed subset of a compact set is compact. To separate ∞\infty∞ from yyy, take a compact-open neighborhood of yyy and its complement. Old points are already Hausdorff separated. Any open cover of DDD has a member containing ∞\infty∞, whose complement is compact in YYY, so it has a finite subcover. Hence DDD is compact Hausdorff. The countable dense subset of YYY from Lemma 3.26 is dense in DDD: YYY is not compact, since it is uncountable and its compact subsets are countable, so every neighborhood of ∞\infty∞ meets YYY. Thus DDD is separable.

The construction has a compact-clopen basis of cardinality at most ℵ1=c\aleph_1=\mathfrak cℵ1​=c: there are only countably many basic sets introduced at each stage. Each such set is clopen in DDD. They separate distinct old points and separate every old point from ∞\infty∞. Their characteristic functions give a continuous injective map D⟶{0,12}I⊂TI,∣I∣≤c.(3.62) D\longrightarrow \{0,\tfrac12\}^{I}\subset\mathbb T^I, \qquad |I|\le\mathfrak c. \tag{3.62} D⟶{0,21​}I⊂TI,∣I∣≤c.(3.62) Specifically use value 1/2+Z1/2+\mathbb Z1/2+Z on the chosen clopen set and zero on its complement. The continuous injection is an embedding because its domain is compact and its range Hausdorff.

Extend η\etaη to the Borel probability ηˉ(B)=η(B∩Y)\bar\eta(B)=\eta(B\cap Y)ηˉ​(B)=η(B∩Y) on DDD. The open set YYY is conull, actual standard, has null singletons, and contains no positive compact subset. Push through (3.62) and apply Proposition 3.20. It gives the separable compact torus KKK, fully supported quasi-invariant probability ν\nuν, and conull standard carrier V=⋃k∈ZYk(3.63) V=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}Y_k \tag{3.63} V=k∈Z⋃​Yk​(3.63) on disjoint compact levels DkD_kDk​, with Yk=V∩DkY_k=V\cap D_kYk​=V∩Dk​ homeomorphic to YYY. Every compact subset of VVV is null by that proposition. This torus action remains nonergodic at this intermediate stage.

It remains to verify the newly required finite-power condition, which was not a conclusion of Proposition 3.20. For fixed rrr, partition VrV^rVr into the countably many disjoint strata Yk1×⋯×Ykr,(k1,…,kr)∈Zr.(3.64) Y_{k_1}\times\cdots\times Y_{k_r}, \qquad (k_1,\ldots,k_r)\in\mathbb Z^r. \tag{3.64} Yk1​​×⋯×Ykr​​,(k1​,…,kr​)∈Zr.(3.64) Each stratum is closed relative to VrV^rVr, since DkD_kDk​ is compact closed in the torus. Each coordinate slice YkY_kYk​ is Borel in VVV. The actual Borel sigma-algebra on a stratum is its coordinate product sigma-algebra by its homeomorphism with YrY^rYr and Theorem 3.27. That product is also the trace of B(V)⊗r\mathcal B(V)^{\otimes r}B(V)⊗r: relative Borel sets in each YkY_kYk​ are Borel in VVV, since YkY_kYk​ is Borel there, and their rectangles generate the trace.

If A⊂VrA\subset V^rA⊂Vr is topologically Borel, each AAA intersected with a stratum is therefore coordinate-product measurable in the whole VrV^rVr. Countably many strata cover the space, so AAA is coordinate-product measurable. Continuous coordinate projections give the reverse inclusion. This proves (3.35) for every rrr, completing every seed hypothesis simultaneously. □\square□

Theorem 3.29 (a standard atomless compact-extraction counterexample under CH). Assume CH. There are a separable compact Hausdorff space XXX, a jointly continuous pointwise free Z\mathbb ZZ-action on XXX, and a fully supported, invariant, ergodic, atomless Borel probability μ\muμ, standard on an actual conull Borel carrier E⊂XE\subset XE⊂X, such that L⊂E compact⟹μ(L)=0.(3.65) L\subset E\ {\rm compact}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mu(L)=0. \tag{3.65} L⊂E compact⟹μ(L)=0.(3.65) Consequently the original topology, separability, and the standing conull-standard measure premise do not yield source Exercise 5(a) in every CH model. Its positive second countable/Radon branch and its measurable wandering conclusions remain valid.

Proof. Proposition 3.28 supplies every hypothesis of Theorem 3.23. Apply that theorem with its actual K,ν,VK,\nu,VK,ν,V: take X=KZ×TX=K^{\mathbb Z}\times\mathbb TX=KZ×T, E=VZ×TE=V^{\mathbb Z}\times\mathbb TE=VZ×T, the independent coordinate probability with circle length, and the shift followed by an irrational circle rotation. Lemmas 3.21–3.22 and that theorem prove all listed properties, including actual standardness of EEE, full support, invariant ergodicity, pointwise freeness on all of XXX, and (3.65). The acting group Z\mathbb ZZ is separable, discrete and locally compact; XXX is separable, compact, locally compact and Hausdorff. The positive set EEE is actual Borel and has mass one. It has no positive compact subset even before a disjointness condition for a nonidentity translate is imposed. This gives the asserted failure.

CH is retained as an additional hypothesis in the entire existence proof. The argument does not claim a ZFC proof that such a counterexample exists without CH. It does show that a universal compact-extraction assertion based only on the stated separability and standard-measure hypotheses cannot remain valid after adjoining CH. The independent full proof of the measurable conclusion in Theorem 3.2, the atomic branch in Theorem 3.5, and the regularity theorem under its stronger topological hypothesis are unchanged. □\square□

Figure 7. Under CH, Lemmas 3.24–3.26 build the locally compact refinement and prove hereditary separability of every finite power. Theorem 3.27 proves actual finite-power Borel equality by intersecting mixed closures; ordinal-order regions are not treated as Borel. Proposition 3.28 compactifies and embeds the space, then repairs support on the disjoint torus levels. Theorem 3.29 applies the already proved Bernoulli and irrational-circle construction: the shift and circle Fourier coefficients give ergodicity, the irrational circle coordinate gives freeness at every ambient point, and compact zeroth-coordinate projection gives zero mass inside the actual conull carrier. This is a proved CH construction; no existence theorem without CH is claimed. De la Vega and Kunen, Theorem 2.4, Section 2, pages 2–3, supplies the related recursive method; the successor details and finite-power Borel proof are given here. Takesaki III, XIII.1, Exercise 5(a), pages 11–12, is the source assertion being tested.

Reading the topological action exercise

The three clauses of Takesaki III, Exercise XIII.1.5 have different conclusions and require different arguments. Its finite measure is quasi-invariant, ergodic and fully supported; the action is jointly continuous and every nonidentity element fixes no point. The group retains the standing separable locally compact convention. The exercise block's topological countability phrase does not explicitly require a countable base for the original space.

Positive compact extraction, part (a). For a finite Radon measure, the earlier compact separation proof, Lemma 2.1, extracts a positive compact subset of every positive Borel set and separates it from its prescribed nonidentity translate. Theorem 1.2 supplies the entire regularity premise when every open set is sigma-compact, in particular for second-countable locally compact spaces. Theorem 3.5 proves all three clauses in the atomic standard branch without that topological premise.

At ordinary separability and conull-standard scope, Theorem 3.29 gives the other outcome assuming CH. Its actual positive Borel carrier contains no positive compact subset, although the compact ambient space, measure and action satisfy all the explicitly stated dynamical conditions. Thus the universal assertion fails under that reading in CH models. This is a qualified negative existence result; it neither identifies the author's intended countability convention nor proves existence without CH. The positive second-countable and Radon assertions retain their complete proofs.

Neighborhood separation, part (b). Supply the omitted parameter as a compact set K⊂G∖{e}K\subset G\setminus\{e\}K⊂G∖{e}, as in Definition XIII.1.3. Given the positive compact set LLL, Lemma 2.2 with E=C=LE=C=LE=C=L supplies x0∈Lx_0\in Lx0​∈L such that every neighborhood meets LLL in positive measure. Lemma 3.1 separates x0x_0x0​ from its compact orbit fragment Kx0Kx_0Kx0​, then uses a finite cover of KKK to produce one neighborhood U0U_0U0​ satisfying U0∩KU0=∅U_0\cap KU_0=\varnothingU0​∩KU0​=∅. The correctly typed containment in the source hint is Kx0⊂VKx_0\subset VKx0​⊂V, where VVV is open in XXX. This implication holds whenever LLL is supplied, including beyond Radon scope.

Measurable freeness, part (c). Theorem 3.2 proves the full conclusion with positive Borel wandering subsets. Ergodicity and full support first give a conull countable union of compact carriers by Theorem 2.1. A positive intersection with one carrier supplies a support point; uniform separation then gives the positive Borel intersection FFF. Compactness of FFF is not required. This proof applies also to the CH model and establishes the measure-algebra projection condition for every prescribed compact KKK avoiding the identity.

Together these arguments complete a scope-separated disposition of Exercise 5. They account for all three clauses without making the conditional separation depend on a universally valid compact-extraction assertion. The eight numbered exercises can now be read through five complete literal proofs, two unconditional corrective dispositions and this one mixed disposition:

  • Exercises 2, 3, 4 and 6 are proved in Compact fixed sets and free Polish models, with the stated ratio-spectrum, compact-model and operator prerequisites.
  • Exercise 8 is proved in Fourier cutoffs and the free diagonal; its compact projection freeness premise yields the full diagonal conclusion.
  • Exercise 1's parameter and coupling assertions receive the complete corrections in Weyl lattices and coupling dimension.
  • Exercise 7's modular formulas and assertions about every original orbit receive the complete corrections and conull replacements in Orbit representatives and null-fibre exceptions.

The block is thereby fully accounted for at these explicit prerequisites. This does not make every printed assertion true, remove CH from the negative branch, or supply all transitive foundational proofs. Each corrected formula and point-model qualification remains part of its proof.

4. Exact examples and the regularity boundary

Example 4.1 (real translations with a finite nonsingular measure). Let G=RG=\mathbb RG=R act on X=RX=\mathbb RX=R by translations and set dμ(x)=12e−∣x∣ dx,K=[−3,−2]∪[2,3],U=(−2/5,2/5).(4.1) d\mu(x)=\tfrac12 e^{-|x|}\,dx,\qquad K=[-3,-2]\cup[2,3],\qquad U=(-2/5,2/5). \tag{4.1} dμ(x)=21​e−∣x∣dx,K=[−3,−2]∪[2,3],U=(−2/5,2/5).(4.1) This measure is a probability with full support. Its strictly positive density makes it equivalent to Lebesgue measure, so every translation is nonsingular. The point action is free, continuous and transitive; every exactly invariant Borel set is empty or the whole line, proving ergodicity.

The exact translates satisfy KU=(−17/5,−8/5)∪(8/5,17/5),KU∩U=∅.(4.2) KU=(-17/5,-8/5)\cup(8/5,17/5),\qquad KU\cap U=\varnothing. \tag{4.2} KU=(−17/5,−8/5)∪(8/5,17/5),KU∩U=∅.(4.2) For the compact set E=[−1/3,1/3]⊂UE=[-1/3,1/3]\subset UE=[−1/3,1/3]⊂U, take F=EF=EF=E. Direct integration gives μ(F)=1−e−1/3>0.(4.3) \mu(F)=1-e^{-1/3}>0. \tag{4.3} μ(F)=1−e−1/3>0.(4.3) Thus the source assumptions and the common compact-family conclusion have a concrete realization. The smallest gap between UUU and KUKUKU is 8/5−2/5=6/58/5-2/5=6/58/5−2/5=6/5.

Example 4.2 (a finite Borel measure with no positive compact subset). Let ω1\omega_1ω1​ be the first uncountable ordinal and Y=[0,ω1)Y=[0,\omega_1)Y=[0,ω1​) with its order topology. A subset D⊂YD\subset YD⊂Y is a club if it is closed and unbounded. Every countable intersection of clubs is a club. To check unboundedness, start above any specified countable ordinal and choose a strictly increasing sequence, at stage nnn choosing its next member in the intersection of the first nnn clubs. Finite intersections are unbounded: alternate choices in the finitely many clubs and take the supremum of that countable increasing sequence. Closedness puts the supremum in every club. The same diagonal argument for all clubs gives a countable supremum below ω1\omega_1ω1​, belonging to each one. Closedness of the intersection is immediate.

Every Borel subset E⊂YE\subset YE⊂Y either contains a club or has a complement containing a club. Indeed the sets having this dichotomy form a sigma-algebra. Complementation is automatic. For a countable union, a member containing a club makes the union positive; if no member does, intersect clubs in their complements to get a club disjoint from the union. Every closed set is in this class: an unbounded closed set is a club, and a bounded closed set has a closed tail in its complement. Therefore all Borel sets have the dichotomy. The two alternatives are exclusive because two clubs intersect.

Define on the Borel sigma-algebra ν(E)={1,E contains a club,0,Y∖E contains a club.(4.4) \nu(E)= \begin{cases} 1,&E\text{ contains a club},\\ 0,&Y\setminus E\text{ contains a club}. \end{cases} \tag{4.4} ν(E)={1,0,​E contains a club,Y∖E contains a club.​(4.4) This is a probability. In a disjoint countable family at most one member contains a club. If one does, its union has measure one; all other members have measure zero. If none does, the intersection of the complement clubs makes the union have measure zero. These two cases prove countable additivity.

Every compact subset of YYY is bounded: the open initial segments [0,α)[0,\alpha)[0,α), α<ω1\alpha<\omega_1α<ω1​, cover YYY; a finite subcover on a compact set gives a countable ordinal bound. A bounded set has club complement and hence measure zero. Thus ν(Y)=1,ν(C)=0 for every compact C⊂Y.(4.5) \nu(Y)=1,\qquad \nu(C)=0\text{ for every compact }C\subset Y. \tag{4.5} ν(Y)=1,ν(C)=0 for every compact C⊂Y.(4.5) The space is locally compact Hausdorff. Closed bounded ordinal intervals are compact: if an interval had an open cover with no finite subcover, the least ordinal whose initial closed interval fails finite coverage is neither a successor nor a limit, since a neighborhood of that endpoint and finitely covered earlier segment give a finite cover. This contradiction proves compactness. Such intervals supply compact neighborhoods of each point.

This example is outside the source exercise. Every countable subset of YYY is bounded, so YYY is not separable. Every point has a bounded open neighborhood of measure zero, so the measure does not have full support. It illustrates why “finite Borel” alone cannot be silently replaced by “finite Radon.”

One may also extend ν\nuν to the compact ordinal interval Z=[0,ω1]Z=[0,\omega_1]Z=[0,ω1​] by giving the last point zero mass. For Borel E⊂ZE\subset ZE⊂Z, set νˉ(E)=ν(E∩Y)\bar\nu(E)=\nu(E\cap Y)νˉ(E)=ν(E∩Y). The Borel set Y⊂ZY\subset ZY⊂Z still has measure one and every compact subset of it has measure zero. Thus even compactness of the ambient space alone does not prove compact inner approximation of its Borel subsets. The only support point of this extended measure is ω1\omega_1ω1​, and its singleton has measure zero.

Example 4.3 (sigma-finite, with no local finiteness). On X=RX=\mathbb RX=R, let μ(E)=#(E∩Q)\mu(E)=\#(E\cap\mathbb Q)μ(E)=#(E∩Q), and let the discrete group Q\mathbb QQ act by translations. The measure is sigma-finite: use rational singletons and the null set of irrationals. It has full support, but every nonempty open interval has infinite measure, so it is not locally finite. The compact sets [−n,n][-n,n][−n,n] cover XXX. Corollary 3.3 applies.

Directly, every positive EEE contains a rational rrr, and F={r}F=\{r\}F={r} has measure one and is disjoint from every nonzero translate. Compact subsets of the discrete group are finite. The action is nonsingular and pointwise free. It is ergodic for this measure because a nonempty invariant set containing one rational contains every rational; otherwise it is null. This example is a sigma-finite extension of the measurable conclusion, not a finite-measure application of Theorem 1.2.

5. Exercises with complete solutions

Level 1 asks for a computation, level 2 for a proof within one mechanism, and level 3 for the combined source-scope argument.

The countable base selects a countable subcover VjV_jVj​: for each basic open set lying in some VxV_xVx​, choose one such VxV_xVx​. Every point lies in a selected set since it lies in a basic open subset of its original VxV_xVx​. Finite unions Cn=⋃j≤nVj‾C_n=\bigcup_{j\le n}\overline{V_j}Cn​=⋃j≤n​Vj​​ are compact, contained in OOO, increasing, and cover OOO. Continuity from below then gives μ(O)=sup⁡nμ(Cn)\mu(O)=\sup_n\mu(C_n)μ(O)=supn​μ(Cn​) for any measure finite on the relevant open set.

Exercise 5.2 (all Borel sets, including completion). Level 2. Complete the passage from inner approximation of open sets to (1.2), without citing a regularity theorem.

Solution. Open inner compact approximation gives outer open approximation of closed sets by taking complements. The class admitting closed/open sandwiches with arbitrarily small gap contains opens and is closed under complements. For a countable union, choose individual gaps with a summable ε2−j−3\varepsilon 2^{-j-3}ε2−j−3 budget. Their open supersets have union with outer error below ε/4\varepsilon/4ε/4. Finiteness chooses a finite initial union of the original sets with omitted measure below ε/4\varepsilon/4ε/4. The corresponding finite union of closed inner approximants is closed and misses measure below ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2. The resulting gap is below ε\varepsilonε. This proves sigma-algebra closure and hence all Borel sandwiches. Intersect the closed inner set with a sufficiently large compact term of the exhaustion of XXX; its discarded tail is arbitrarily small, yielding (1.2). For a completion-measurable set choose a Borel subset of equal measure and approximate that subset from inside, so the compact approximants lie in the actual completed set.

No compact approximation of a Borel subset of GCGCGC was used.

Exercise 5.6 (exact translation geometry). Level 1. Verify every assertion in Example 4.1, including the two translate intervals, the gap and the probability of F=[−1/3,1/3]F=[-1/3,1/3]F=[−1/3,1/3].

Solution. The density integrates to one because its two half-line integrals are 1/21/21/2. It is positive everywhere, so it has the Lebesgue null sets and full support; translations preserve the measure class. The real translation action is continuous, free and transitive, which makes every exactly invariant set empty or all of R\mathbb RR. Minkowski addition of the intervals gives [−3,−2]+(−2/5,2/5)=(−17/5,−8/5)[-3,-2]+(-2/5,2/5)=(-17/5,-8/5)[−3,−2]+(−2/5,2/5)=(−17/5,−8/5) and [2,3]+(−2/5,2/5)=(8/5,17/5)[2,3]+(-2/5,2/5)=(8/5,17/5)[2,3]+(−2/5,2/5)=(8/5,17/5). Its translates by every member of KKK are therefore disjoint from it.

Exercise 5.7 (sigma-finite carriers). Level 3. Prove Corollary 3.3 and verify all the hypotheses and conclusions of Example 4.3.

Solution. From a finite-measure cover HjH_jHj​ and compact conull cover CnC_nCn​, some intersection E∩Hj∩CnE\cap H_j\cap C_nE∩Hj​∩Cn​ has finite positive measure. Apply the finite compact support-point proof to that intersection, uniformly separate its support point from the compact orbit fragment, and intersect the wandering neighborhood with that same Borel intersection. This proves the corollary. Counting rational points is countably additive and sigma-finite, with the irrational set null; every interval contains infinitely many rational points, so local finiteness fails and support is full. Rational translations permute the counted points, so preserve the measure, and fix no real point when nonzero. The compact intervals cover XXX. Every positive set contains a rational rrr; its singleton has measure one and misses all nonzero translates. An exactly invariant set either contains no rational and is null, or contains the entire rational orbit and is conull. This proves ergodicity and every claimed measured conclusion.

Solution. Closed unbounded subsets of the countable ordinals remain closed unbounded under countable intersections, by alternating finite-club choices and the diagonal countable-supremum construction. The class of sets containing a club or having club complement is a sigma-algebra containing all closed sets, so every Borel set has exactly one of these alternatives. In a disjoint countable family at most one member contains a club; if none does, intersect the complement clubs. These two cases prove countable additivity of (4.4) and total mass one. A compact subset is bounded by a finite subcover of the open initial-segment cover and has measure zero. Closed bounded ordinal intervals are compact by the least-failing-initial-interval argument, so the ordinal space is locally compact Hausdorff. Countable sets are bounded, so it is not separable; bounded neighborhoods have measure zero, so full support fails. Extending the last point with zero mass yields the compact-space version of the same failure of inner approximation on the Borel subset YYY.

The example does not refute Exercise 5 under its standing hypotheses. Here part (c) has a complete proof under the printed finite, ergodic, full-support, quasi-invariant assumptions and the standing separable group convention, without Radon regularity or a countable base for XXX. Part (b) is completely proved whenever the stated compact positive LLL is given, with the intended compact KKK written explicitly. Part (a), and consequently the entire compact-extraction route, is completely proved when every open subset of XXX is sigma-compact or a finite Radon measure is given. The source's general countability wording is not asserted to be an explicit countable-base hypothesis. Theorem 3.5 also proves the atomic standard branch. Theorem 3.29 supplies an actual atomless counterexample under CH at the ordinary-separability and conull-standard scope. These results complete a qualified disposition of the exercise; they do not identify the author's intended stronger countability convention or prove counterexample existence without CH.

The countable discrete space is Polish and its Borel sigma-algebra is its full power set, so the measure is standard on the original point space. μ(2Z)=13(1+2∑k≥14−k)=59.(5.1) \mu(2\mathbb Z)=\frac13\left(1+2\sum_{k\ge1}4^{-k}\right) =\frac59. \tag{5.1} μ(2Z)=31​(1+2k≥1∑​4−k)=95​.(5.1) The singleton L={0}L=\{0\}L={0} is a compact subset of 2Z2\mathbb Z2Z, has mass 1/31/31/3, and m+L={m}m+L=\{m\}m+L={m} misses LLL for every nonzero integer mmm. This is one choice working for all such elements, hence for each compact parameter family.

Exercise 5.10 (why an algebraic atom is insufficient). Level 3. Compare Lemma 3.4 with the nonregular compact-action example in Separable compact actions with nonregular measures, Propositions 4.1–4.2. For each jjj, the atom condition chooses a side CjC_jCj​ of BjB_jBj​ for which Dn∩S∩CjD_n\cap S\cap C_jDn​∩S∩Cj​ has the full mass of DnD_nDn​. The intersection F=Dn∩S∩⋂jCjF=D_n\cap S\cap\bigcap_jC_jF=Dn​∩S∩⋂j​Cj​ still has that positive mass by countable subadditivity. Point separation makes FFF contain at most one point. Its separable atomic measure algebra does not supply the point-space premise of Lemma 3.4. Theorem 3.5 proves the source exercise's atomic standard-measure branch. An unconditional existence theorem without CH is not claimed.
