Exercise 5.13 (why ergodicity matters). Level 3. Let (Y,ν)(Y,\nu)(Y,ν) be the compact integer-action example in Separable compact actions with nonregular measures, with its conull Borel E0E_0E0​ containing no positive compact subset. Take X=T⊔Y,μ=12λT+12ν.(5.2) X=\mathbb T\sqcup Y,\qquad \mu=\tfrac12\lambda_{\mathbb T}+\tfrac12\nu. \tag{5.2} X=T⊔Y,μ=21​λT​+21​ν.(5.2) Let n∈Zn\in\mathbb Zn∈Z rotate the circle by n(2−1)n(\sqrt2-1)n(2​−1) and act on YYY by the existing translations. Verify the topological and measure-class properties. Determine the maximal Radon part RRR, and explain which hypothesis of Theorem 3.10 fails.

Solution. A finite disjoint union of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact Hausdorff, and both components are open and closed. Their countable dense sets give a countable dense set in XXX. The circle rotation is continuous and pointwise free because 2−1\sqrt2-12​−1 is irrational; the action on YYY has these properties by its full construction. Both summands have total mass one before the factor 1/21/21/2, so μ(X)=1\mu(X)=1μ(X)=1. Haar measure on the circle is rotation invariant and has full support; ν\nuν is quasi-invariant with full support. Thus the sum is quasi-invariant and has full support.

The circle is second countable, so Theorem 1.2 makes it a Radon part. No Radon part can have positive mass in YYY: its intersection with the conull E0E_0E0​ would be positive and, by regularity, would contain a positive compact subset. This contradicts the defining property of E0E_0E0​. Proposition 3.8 therefore gives R=T(modμ-null sets),μ(R)=12.(5.3) R=\mathbb T\pmod{\mu\text{-null sets}},\qquad \mu(R)=\tfrac12. \tag{5.3} R=T(modμ-null sets),μ(R)=21​.(5.3) Both components are exactly invariant and have mass 1/21/21/2, so the action is not ergodic. This explains the intermediate mass without contradicting Theorem 3.10. The YYY-component does not have a conull standard Borel point space; none is asserted for this example.

Exercise 5.14 (positive compact mass versus a regular part). Level 3. In the original compact nonregular integer-action example, the whole space YYY is compact and has mass one. Show nevertheless that its maximal Radon part is null. Then explain what must be established to obtain source Exercise 5(a) from Theorem 3.10 at the standing atomless standard-measure scope.

Solution. If A⊂YA\subset YA⊂Y were a positive Radon part, A∩E0A\cap E_0A∩E0​ would be a positive Borel subset of AAA. Compact inner approximation would give a positive compact subset of E0E_0E0​, which is impossible. Hence every Radon part is null, and the maximal part has mass zero. The compact set YYY has positive mass, but its restricted measure is nonregular. Positive compact mass alone therefore does not select the Radon branch.

At the standing standard-measure source scope, it suffices to prove that some positive Borel AAA has positive compact extraction for every positive Borel subset of AAA. Lemma 3.7 makes this a Radon part; transport and ergodicity then make the entire measure Radon, and Corollary 3.11 proves 5(a). Conversely, an actual source counterexample must realize the other branch with all the free, ergodic, full-support, quasi-invariant and standard point-space hypotheses. The earlier nonregular example lacks the last hypothesis; a measure-only nonregular construction would still need a verified dynamical action. Neither settles the remaining decision.

Exercise 5.15 (support is invariant but can be null). Level 2. Prove Lemma 3.13 for arbitrary equivalent finite Borel measures, then prove all assertions of Proposition 3.14. Explain why compactness and exact invariance of the support do not give a conull carrier in this example.

Solution. An open neighborhood has zero measure for one of two equivalent measures exactly when it has zero measure for the other, so their supports agree. Pullback of neighborhoods under a homeomorphism proves the transport formula, and nonsingularity then gives exact invariance. The complement is open; if the support were empty on a compact space, finitely many null open neighborhoods would cover the space, contradicting positive total mass. For each y∈Yy\in Yy∈Y, its neighborhood meets DDD countably, hence in a null set; its portion outside DDD is also null because Y⊂DY\subset DY⊂D is conull. Points outside DDD have the null open neighborhood X∖DX\setminus DX∖D. Consequently the support lies in D∖YD\setminus YD∖Y and is null. Its complement is a conull open union of null open sets. A compact subset of YYY has a finite cover by the UyU_yUy​'s, so is countable and null. Ergodicity allows an invariant closed set to be null; exact invariance alone does not decide which alternative occurs. Restricting to this support gives zero mass. □\square□

Exercise 5.16 (dense atoms repair support and defeat ergodicity). Level 2. In Corollary 3.15, take cn=2−nc_n=2^{-n}cn​=2−n and t=1/3t=1/3t=1/3. Verify normalization, full support, the exact mass of the positive-point set, and the compact-subset obstruction on Y∖QY\setminus QY∖Q. Show that no nonsingular homeomorphism action can make this probability ergodic.

Solution. The geometric series is ∑n≥12−n=1\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}=1∑n≥1​2−n=1, so η\etaη and λ=(2/3)μ+(1/3)η\lambda=(2/3)\mu+(1/3)\etaλ=(2/3)μ+(1/3)η are probabilities. Every nonempty open set contains a qnq_nqn​, giving λ(U)≥2−n/3>0\lambda(U)\ge 2^{-n}/3>0λ(U)≥2−n/3>0. Since μ\muμ has no positive singleton, precisely the points of QQQ have positive singleton mass and λ(Q)=1/3\lambda(Q)=1/3λ(Q)=1/3. Nonsingularity preserves null singletons in both directions, so every action element maps QQQ onto itself. This exactly invariant Borel set has intermediate measure, disproving ergodicity. The set Y∖QY\setminus QY∖Q has mass 2/32/32/3; each of its compact subsets is countable and misses QQQ, so both measures in the mixture vanish on it. Thus full support has been supplied while the ergodicity requirement remains unsatisfied. □\square□

Exercise 5.17 (quantitative quasi-invariance). Level 2. For a Z\mathbb ZZ-action in (3.20), take cn=2−∣n∣/3c_n=2^{-|n|}/3cn​=2−∣n∣/3. Prove, for every Borel BBB and integer kkk, 2−∣k∣μ(B)≤μ(τkB)≤2∣k∣μ(B).(5.4) 2^{-|k|}\mu(B)\le\mu(\tau_kB)\le2^{|k|}\mu(B). \tag{5.4} 2−∣k∣μ(B)≤μ(τk​B)≤2∣k∣μ(B).(5.4) Show that any exactly invariant Borel event has the same mass for the seed and mixture. Explain why none of this proves ergodicity for an atomless seed.

Solution. Formula (3.23) gives νn(τkB)=νn−k(B)\nu_n(\tau_kB)=\nu_{n-k}(B)νn​(τk​B)=νn−k​(B). Substitute m=n−km=n-km=n−k to obtain μ(τkB)=∑mcm+kνm(B)\mu(\tau_kB)=\sum_mc_{m+k}\nu_m(B)μ(τk​B)=∑m​cm+k​νm​(B). The triangle inequality gives −∣k∣≤∣m∣−∣m+k∣≤∣k∣-|k|\le |m|-|m+k|\le|k|−∣k∣≤∣m∣−∣m+k∣≤∣k∣. Therefore 2−∣k∣≤cm+k/cm≤2∣k∣2^{-|k|}\le c_{m+k}/c_m\le2^{|k|}2−∣k∣≤cm+k​/cm​≤2∣k∣. Multiply by the nonnegative cmνm(B)c_m\nu_m(B)cm​νm​(B) and sum to prove (5.4), including null sets. For exactly invariant BBB, every τ−nB=B\tau_{-n}B=Bτ−n​B=B, so each νn(B)=ν(B)\nu_n(B)=\nu(B)νn​(B)=ν(B), and normalization gives μ(B)=ν(B)\mu(B)=\nu(B)μ(B)=ν(B). An atomless seed admits sets of intermediate mass; the calculation does not show that their saturations must be null or conull. In Proposition 3.20 the saturation of any intermediate seed event is exactly invariant with that same mass. Thus bounded comparison of translates, full support, and atomlessness do not replace the ergodicity check. □\square□

Exercise 5.18 (all compact subsets of the new carrier). Level 3. Under Proposition 3.20's seed hypotheses, prove directly that the actual conull Borel set E=⋃nYnE=\bigcup_nY_nE=⋃n​Yn​ is standard Borel and that every compact L⊂EL\subset EL⊂E is μ\muμ-null. Verify that every positive Borel AAA contains a positive Borel subset with no positive compact subset. Distinguish the last assertion from the false assertion that every compact subset of XXX is null.

Solution. Each DnD_nDn​ is compact and closed in XXX, and YnY_nYn​ is a Borel standard Borel subset of it. Distinct first-coordinate levels make the pieces disjoint. The relative sigma-algebra on EEE is exactly their countable disjoint-union sigma-algebra: restriction gives one inclusion; countable unions of the Borel pieces give the other. Thus EEE is standard Borel, Borel in XXX, and conull for every term of the mixture and for μ\muμ.

For compact L⊂EL\subset EL⊂E, closedness of DnD_nDn​ makes L∩DnL\cap D_nL∩Dn​ compact. Disjointness makes it a subset of YnY_nYn​. Its inverse image in DDD is a compact subset of YYY, hence seed-null. Since νn\nu_nνn​ is carried by DnD_nDn​, this proves νn(L)=0\nu_n(L)=0νn​(L)=0 for each nnn and then μ(L)=0\mu(L)=0μ(L)=0. Given positive Borel AAA, its intersection A∩EA\cap EA∩E is Borel with μ(A∩E)=μ(A)>0\mu(A\cap E)=\mu(A)>0μ(A∩E)=μ(A)>0. Any compact subset of that intersection lies in EEE and is null. On the other hand, the whole XXX is compact and μ(X)=1\mu(X)=1μ(X)=1. Compact inner approximation fails on the particular conull Borel carrier and its positive subsets; it does not remove positive mass from every ambient compact set. □\square□

Exercise 5.19 (null overlap already obstructs ergodicity). Level 3. Assume (3.30), and choose Borel A⊂YA\subset YA⊂Y with ν(A)=t∈(0,1)\nu(A)=t\in(0,1)ν(A)=t∈(0,1). The translates of YYY need not be disjoint as sets. Prove that [A]G[A]_G[A]G​ is exactly invariant and has μ\muμ-mass ttt. For t=1/2t=1/2t=1/2, compute the masses of this event and its complement. Explain why declaring each μ\muμ-translate carrier a copy of a nonatomic probability space does not make the action ergodic.

Solution. Left multiplication permutes GGG, so h[A]G=[A]Gh[A]_G=[A]_Gh[A]G​=[A]G​ for every hhh. The portion ([A]G∩Y)∖A([A]_G\cap Y)\setminus A([A]G​∩Y)∖A is contained in ⋃g≠e(gY∩Y)\bigcup_{g\ne e}(gY\cap Y)⋃g=e​(gY∩Y). Each term is seed-null by (3.30), and countability gives zero measure for their union. Hence ν([A]G)=ν([A]G∩Y)=t\nu([A]_G)=\nu([A]_G\cap Y)=tν([A]G​)=ν([A]G​∩Y)=t. Exact invariance makes νg([A]G)=ν([A]G)=t\nu_g([A]_G)=\nu([A]_G)=tνg​([A]G​)=ν([A]G​)=t for every ggg, so the weighted sum is ttt. Its complement has mass 1−t1-t1−t, equal to 1/21/21/2 when t=1/2t=1/2t=1/2. The counterevent comes from transporting the same seed event along every carrier. Nonatomicity concerns subdivision of events; ergodicity concerns the absence of invariant intermediate events. Null overlap permits all the seed subdivisions to survive as invariant saturations. Positive returns, with the exact criterion of Theorem 3.19, must be checked. □\square□

Exercise 5.20 (which null ideal can be saturated?). Level 3. Let X=T×{0,1}X=\mathbb T\times\{0,1\}X=T×{0,1}, let the two-element group swap the second coordinate, and let ν=ℓ⊗δ0\nu=\ell\otimes\delta_0ν=ℓ⊗δ0​, where ℓ\ellℓ is circle length probability. Give both group elements weight 1/21/21/2. Compute the mixture, the seed mass of N=T×{1}N=\mathbb T\times\{1\}N=T×{1}, and the masses of its saturation. Then prove for a general countable orbit mixture that saturation of a μ\muμ-null Borel set is μ\muμ-null. Explain the choice of measure in Theorem 3.19's exactification step.

Solution. The swap sends the seed to ℓ⊗δ1\ell\otimes\delta_1ℓ⊗δ1​. Thus μ=(1/2)(ℓ⊗δ0)+(1/2)(ℓ⊗δ1)\mu=(1/2)(\ell\otimes\delta_0)+(1/2)(\ell\otimes\delta_1)μ=(1/2)(ℓ⊗δ0​)+(1/2)(ℓ⊗δ1​). The set NNN has ν(N)=0\nu(N)=0ν(N)=0 and μ(N)=1/2\mu(N)=1/2μ(N)=1/2, while its saturation is XXX, of mass one for both measures. So seed-null exceptional sets are not safe to saturate. This compact standard Borel example is a null-ideal diagnostic; it is not a nonregular or ergodic source example.

For a general mixture, μ(B)=0\mu(B)=0μ(B)=0 implies μ(gB)=0\mu(gB)=0μ(gB)=0 for all ggg, by quasi-invariance in Lemma 3.16. Countable subadditivity gives μ([B]G)=0\mu([B]_G)=0μ([B]G​)=0. Equivalently, (3.21) first gives ν([B]G)=0\nu([B]_G)=0ν([B]G​)=0, and exact invariance of that saturation gives μ([B]G)=ν([B]G)=0\mu([B]_G)=\nu([B]_G)=0μ([B]G​)=ν([B]G​)=0. Therefore replacing a modulo-invariant event by ⋂ggB\bigcap_g gB⋂g​gB preserves its class for μ\muμ. Using the seed's null sets for that replacement without a separate quasi-invariance proof would fail, as the explicit NNN shows. □\square□

Exercise 5.21 (the dynamical repair does not produce the seed). Level 2. Take K=Y={0,1}K=Y=\{0,1\}K=Y={0,1} with discrete topology and probabilities 1/2,1/21/2,1/21/2,1/2. Form (3.43)–(3.46). Verify full support, strong standardness, invariance, pointwise freeness, atomlessness and ergodicity. Exhibit a positive compact cylinder. Identify exactly which seed hypothesis in Theorem 3.23 fails.

Solution. Finite discrete spaces and their finite powers have every subset Borel, so (3.35) holds. The countable binary product with the circle is compact metric and standard Borel. Lemma 3.22 gives independent fair coordinates and mixing of the shift; the Fourier proof (3.48)–(3.49) proves ergodicity after adding the irrational rotation. Product invariance proves invariance. A nonempty finite binary cylinder restricting rrr distinct coordinates, paired with a nonempty circle arc JJJ, has mass 2−rℓ(J)>02^{-r}\ell(J)>02−rℓ(J)>0, proving full support. The circle coordinate gives zero mass to every singleton, and Lemma 3.4 proves atomlessness on the standard space. If TnT^nTn fixes any point, then nα∈Zn\alpha\in\mathbb Znα∈Z, so n=0n=0n=0, proving pointwise freeness even at constant binary sequences.

The set C={x∈{0,1}Z:x0=0}×T C=\{x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}:x_0=0\}\times\mathbb T C={x∈{0,1}Z:x0​=0}×T is a closed subset of the compact space, hence compact, and has mass 1/21/21/2. Also E=XE=XE=X itself is compact of mass one. The missing seed hypothesis is precisely that every compact subset of YYY is ν\nuν-null: already the compact singleton {0}\{0\}{0} has mass 1/21/21/2, and YYY has mass one. Thus the dynamical mechanism supplies all its asserted dynamics here, but cannot supply the compact-extraction obstruction. □\square□

Exercise 5.22 (one standard Borel factor need not have product-Borel powers). Level 3. Let S=RS=\mathbb RS=R with the lower-limit topology generated by intervals [a,b)[a,b)[a,b), a<ba<ba<b. Prove that B(S)\mathcal B(S)B(S) is exactly the usual real Borel sigma-algebra, yet B(S2)≠B(S)⊗B(S). \mathcal B(S^2)\ne\mathcal B(S)\otimes\mathcal B(S). B(S2)=B(S)⊗B(S). Give an explicit form of a set witnessing the difference. Explain the relevance to the last hypothesis of Theorem 3.23 without claiming this space is a compact seed.

Solution. Every usual open interval is lower-limit open, giving one sigma-algebra inclusion. For the reverse, let UUU be lower-limit open and OOO its usual interior. For every x∈U∖Ox\in U\setminus Ox∈U∖O, choose εx>0\varepsilon_x>0εx​>0 with [x,x+εx)⊂U[x,x+\varepsilon_x)\subset U[x,x+εx​)⊂U. Then (x,x+εx)⊂O(x,x+\varepsilon_x)\subset O(x,x+εx​)⊂O. If x<yx<yx<y are both in U∖OU\setminus OU∖O, then y≥x+εxy\ge x+\varepsilon_xy≥x+εx​, since otherwise yyy would lie in OOO. Hence these nonempty open intervals are pairwise disjoint. Choose a rational in each; this injects U∖OU\setminus OU∖O into the rationals and proves it countable. Thus U=O∪(U∖O)U=O\cup(U\setminus O)U=O∪(U∖O) is usual Borel. The two one-factor Borel sigma-algebras agree, so the actual Borel space SSS is standard.

The antidiagonal A={(t,−t):t∈R} A=\{(t,-t):t\in\mathbb R\} A={(t,−t):t∈R} is usual closed and hence closed in the finer product topology of S2S^2S2. It is discrete in that topology: for ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, [t,t+ε)×[−t,−t+ε) ∩A={(t,−t)}. [t,t+\varepsilon)\times[-t,-t+\varepsilon) \ \cap A=\{(t,-t)\}. [t,t+ε)×[−t,−t+ε) ∩A={(t,−t)}. Every subset of a discrete space is relatively closed, so every subset of the closed AAA is closed in S2S^2S2.

Choose a non-Borel subset V⊂RV\subset\mathbb RV⊂R. Such a set exists because there are only continuum many usual Borel sets, obtained by countable Borel codes, and strictly more subsets of R\mathbb RR by Cantor's theorem. The set AV={(t,−t):t∈V} A_V=\{(t,-t):t\in V\} AV​={(t,−t):t∈V} is closed, hence Borel, in S2S^2S2. The product sigma-algebra B(S)⊗B(S)\mathcal B(S)\otimes\mathcal B(S)B(S)⊗B(S) is the usual Borel sigma-algebra of R2\mathbb R^2R2, because the usual topology has a countable rectangular base. If AVA_VAV​ belonged to it, its inverse image under the usual continuous map t↦(t,−t)t\mapsto(t,-t)t↦(t,−t) would be the usual Borel set VVV, a contradiction. Continuous coordinate projections always give the other inclusion, so this is a strict enlargement of the product sigma-algebra.

This example proves that actual one-factor standardness alone cannot justify (3.35). It supplies neither a compact KKK nor the fully supported compact seed measure required by Theorem 3.23, and therefore supplies no source counterexample. □\square□

Exercise 5.23 (the ordinal partition is not a measurable argument). Level 3. Under CH, enumerate the Cantor set as C={cξ:ξ<ω1}C=\{c_\xi:\xi<\omega_1\}C={cξ​:ξ<ω1​}, give it ordinary fair-coin probability η\etaη, and put W={(cα,cβ):α<β}. W=\{(c_\alpha,c_\beta):\alpha<\beta\}. W={(cα​,cβ​):α<β}. Compute the two iterated integrals of its indicator, using its measurable one-coordinate sections. Prove that WWW is not ordinary product-Borel. Explain why Lemma 3.26 can use this ordering to prove separability, while Theorem 3.27 cannot use it as a Borel partition.

Solution. For fixed cβc_\betacβ​ in the second coordinate, the first-coordinate section has the countably many indices α<β\alpha<\betaα<β. It has η\etaη-mass zero. For fixed cαc_\alphacα​ in the first coordinate, the second-coordinate section is the complement of the countable initial segment with indices β≤α\beta\le\alphaβ≤α. It has mass one. All these sections are ordinary Borel, so both iterated integrals are meaningful and give ∫Cη(W y) dη(y)=0,∫Cη(Wx) dη(x)=1. \begin{aligned} \int_C\eta(W^{\,y})\,d\eta(y)&=0,\\ \int_C\eta(W_x)\,d\eta(x)&=1. \end{aligned} ∫C​η(Wy)dη(y)∫C​η(Wx​)dη(x)​=0,=1.​ If WWW were product-Borel, Tonelli for its nonnegative indicator would make these two values equal. They are different, so WWW is not product-Borel. The same reasoning excludes measurability for the completed product probability, since completed-product Fubini still applies to almost all its sections, which already have the stated values everywhere.

Hereditary separability concerns arbitrary subspaces, so it may partition a set by arbitrary ordinal-order patterns and choose a countable dense subset of each one. It needs no measurable partition. A proof of Borel measurability cannot invoke that partition without additional justification, and the explicit WWW shows why. Theorem 3.27 instead takes the intersection of every mixed-coordinate closure. The largest ordinal coordinate is selected only to verify the equality outside the ordinary repeated-coordinate diagonals and a countable exceptional set; no ordinal-order subset enters its Borel-set formula. □\square□

Exercise 5.24 (exact mass and exact compact failure in the CH model). Level 2. In Proposition 3.28 take the weights ck=2−∣k∣/3c_k=2^{-|k|}/3ck​=2−∣k∣/3 from Proposition 3.20, so the total intermediate carrier is V=⋃kYkV=\bigcup_kY_kV=⋃k​Yk​. In the final space of Theorem 3.29, consider the Borel event B={(x,z)∈E:  x0∈Y0, x1∈Y1,z∈[0,12)+Z}. \begin{aligned} B=\{(x,z)\in E:\;&x_0\in Y_0,\ x_1\in Y_1,\\ &z\in[0,\tfrac12)+\mathbb Z\}. \end{aligned} B={(x,z)∈E:​x0​∈Y0​, x1​∈Y1​,z∈[0,21​)+Z}.​ Compute μ(B)\mu(B)μ(B). Prove that every compact subset of BBB has mass zero, while the ambient compact XXX has mass one. State which dynamical and standard-measure source hypotheses hold and which extra set-theoretic premise was used.

Solution. The intermediate levels are disjoint and the translated seed assigns mass one to its own YkY_kYk​, so ν(Yk)=ck\nu(Y_k)=c_kν(Yk​)=ck​. In particular ν(Y0)=1/3\nu(Y_0)=1/3ν(Y0​)=1/3 and ν(Y1)=1/6\nu(Y_1)=1/6ν(Y1​)=1/6. Independence of the zeroth and first coordinates and of circle length gives μ(B)=13⋅16⋅12=136. \mu(B)=\frac13\cdot\frac16\cdot\frac12=\frac1{36}. μ(B)=31​⋅61​⋅21​=361​. The intersections defining BBB are actual Borel: the level sets are Borel in KKK, the coordinate maps are continuous, the circle half-arc is Borel, and EEE is ambient Borel.

If L⊂BL\subset BL⊂B is compact, then L⊂EL\subset EL⊂E, so its zeroth-coordinate projection is a compact subset of the conull intermediate VVV. Proposition 3.28 makes that projection ν\nuν-null, and (3.50) makes LLL μ\muμ-null. Thus this explicitly positive event contains no positive compact subset. The whole XXX is compact and has mass one; the claim concerns compact subsets of the particular Borel carrier, not all ambient compact sets.

The acting group is countable discrete Z\mathbb ZZ, hence separable and locally compact. The ambient space is separable compact Hausdorff, hence locally compact. The action is jointly continuous, free at every point, and preserves a finite ergodic atomless fully supported Borel probability. Its actual invariant conull carrier is standard Borel. The additional premise is CH, used to enumerate all countable finite-power closure requirements in an ω1\omega_1ω1​ recursion. It is not a conclusion of the source assumptions. The construction therefore gives the stated CH counterexample and makes no unconditional ZFC existence claim. □\square□

References and source scope

[Takesaki III] Masamichi Takesaki, Theory of Operator Algebras III, Encyclopaedia of Mathematical Sciences 127, Springer, 2003. XIII.1, standing group/measure assumptions and Definition 1.3; Exercise 5 and exercise-block countability convention, pages 11–12. Publisher record.

[Takesaki I] Masamichi Takesaki, Theory of Operator Algebras I, first edition, 1979. Appendix, definition immediately before Corollary A.14, printed page 383 / PDF page 390 in the supplied edition: deletion of a null set leaves a standard Borel point space. This is the exact definition compared for the conull-standard interpretation. Lemma 3.4 supplies the full atom-to-point proof.

[Fremlin] D. H. Fremlin, Measure Theory, Volume 4, Chapter 43, §433C and §433X(e), provides related general results on analytic Hausdorff topologies and on abstract standard Borel measure spaces. The abstract measurable-space statement concerns a suitable topology; it is not used to change the topology of the source exercise. Our elementary regularity proof is Theorem 1.2. Only the indicated bounded passages were consulted; the analytic-space and perfect-measure foundations are not claimed proved or imported here. Author's Chapter 43.

[de la Vega–Kunen] Ramiro de la Vega and Kenneth Kunen, A Compact Homogeneous S-space, arXiv:math/0303239v1, 19 March 2003. Theorem 2.4, Section 2, pages 2–3, gives the CH topological recursion. Lemmas 3.24–3.26 give the full successor construction and the global mixed-topology induction; Theorem 3.27 supplies the further Borel equality needed here. The later homogeneity results are not used. Primary paper.

[Wage] M. L. Wage, Products of Radon spaces, Russian Mathematical Surveys 35:3 (1980), 185–187. The three-page construction's reported diagonal properties were compared with Proposition 3.14; its omitted inductive verification is not imported. Primary journal record.

The prior finite Radon proof remains unchanged. This lesson closes the full measurable conclusion independently of compact inner regularity and supplies the full regularity theorem at its explicit topological scope. Lemma 3.4 and Theorem 3.5 now prove the atomic standard-measure branch of all three clauses. Theorem 3.29 now gives a full atomless standard-measure counterexample in the original topology under CH. Exercise 5 and the eight-exercise block have complete qualified dispositions at the stated prerequisites: five literal exercise proofs, two corrective dispositions, and the mixed disposition of Exercise 5 explained above. The intended stronger countability convention is not inferred; existence without CH is not claimed. The remaining five-unit assignment stays open.
